panels.title: CPU Usage
panels.description: Displays the percentage of CPU currently utilized by the server. The value is calculated by subtracting idle CPU time from total CPU time over a five minute interval. Sustained CPU utilization above eighty percent may indicate CPU saturation, increased response latency, or insufficient compute resources.

panels.title: Memory Usage
panels.description: Displays the percentage of physical memory currently being used. The metric compares available memory against total installed memory. Sustained high memory utilization may result in swapping, reduced performance, or application instability.

panels.title: Disk Usage %
panels.description: Displays the percentage of persistent storage currently in use on the system disk. Temporary file systems are excluded. High disk utilization may prevent applications from writing files, logs, or database data.

panels.title: System Uptime
panels.description: Displays the amount of time the operating system has been running since the last reboot. Sudden decreases usually indicate server restarts or crashes.

panels.title: Network Receive Throughput
panels.description: Measures inbound network traffic received by the server excluding the loopback interface. Useful for monitoring traffic spikes and bandwidth utilization.

panels.title: Network Transmit Throughput
panels.description: Measures outbound network traffic transmitted by the server excluding loopback traffic. Useful for monitoring API responses, uploads, and communication with external systems.

panels.title: Disk Read IOPS
panels.description: Displays the number of completed disk read operations per second. Useful for identifying storage intensive workloads and database read activity.

panels.title: Disk Write IOPS
panels.description: Displays the number of completed disk write operations per second. High write rates may indicate intensive logging, backups, or database write activity.

panels.title: System Load Average
panels.description: Displays the one minute system load average. Values consistently greater than the available CPU cores may indicate CPU contention or resource saturation.

panels.title: HTTP Request Rate
panels.description: this shows all the HTTP request that are coming towards or going out of the website

panels.title: LOGS
panels.description: This is the logs of crypto wallet you can see all the details of backend using these logs. You can also see any specific kind of data by clicking on log level

panels.title: HTTP Requests per Second
panels.description: Displays the total number of HTTP requests processed per second across all endpoints. This metric represents the overall traffic entering the backend service and is useful for identifying traffic spikes and sudden drops in activity.

panels.title: Active HTTP Requests
panels.description: Displays the number of requests currently being processed by the backend. A continuously increasing value may indicate slow requests, thread starvation, or application bottlenecks.

panels.title: Average Request Duration
panels.description: Displays the average request processing time over the last five minutes. This metric provides a general overview of backend responsiveness.

panels.title: HTTP Error Rate
panels.description: Displays the percentage of failed HTTP requests (5xx responses). A sustained increase indicates application failures or backend instability.

panels.title: P50 Response Time
panels.description: Shows the response time experienced by 50% of all requests. Useful for understanding normal application performance.

panels.title: P90 Response Time
panels.description: Shows the response time experienced by 90% of requests. Helps detect moderate latency increases before they affect most users.

panels.title: P95 Response Time
panels.description: Industry standard latency metric used for SRE monitoring. Represents the response time experienced by 95% of requests.

panels.title: P99 Response Time
panels.description: Displays tail latency. High P99 latency usually indicates performance bottlenecks affecting a small subset of requests.

panels.title: HTTP Status Code Distribution
panels.description: Shows the distribution of HTTP response codes (2xx, 3xx, 4xx, and 5xx). Useful for identifying increases in client or server errors.

panels.title: Endpoint Latency
panels.description: Displays the P95 response time for each API endpoint. Makes it easy to identify the slowest endpoints.

panels.title: Endpoint Throughput
panels.description: Displays request throughput for every endpoint. Useful for identifying the most heavily used APIs.

panels.title: Database Query Throughput
panels.description: Displays the number of SQL queries executed per second, calculated from the existing db_query_duration_count counter already instrumented in the application (the same metric family powering the Database Queries and Average Query Latency panels). A sudden increase indicates heavier database activity, while an unexpected decrease may indicate application issues or database outages.

panels.title: Average Query Latency
panels.description: Displays the average execution time of SQL queries over the selected time range, calculated by dividing the rate of total query duration by the rate of total query count over a 5 minute window (sum/count average). Rising latency often indicates slow queries, insufficient indexing, lock contention, or increased system load. Uses the same db_query_duration_* metric family already instrumented on the Database Queries panel.

panels.title: P95 Query Latency
panels.description: Displays the 95th percentile query latency: the execution time experienced by the slowest five percent of database queries. Calculated using histogram_quantile against the db_query_duration_bucket histogram, which groups query durations into cumulative latency buckets. This is the preferred SRE metric for database performance because it exposes tail latency without being distorted by the majority of fast queries.

panels.title: Database Health Score
panels.description: A derived composite health indicator combining five underlying signals: P95 query latency exceeding 500ms, any query running longer than 30s, any deadlocks in the last hour, any active lock waits, and connection pool utilization exceeding 90%. Each true condition contributes one point to the score (0-5). A score of 0 is mapped to Healthy (green), 1-2 to Warning (yellow), and 3 or more to Critical (red). This gives an at-a-glance rollup of database health without needing to check every individual panel during an incident.

targets.expr: ((clamp_max(count(pg_running_queries_duration_seconds > 30) or vector(0), 1)) + ((histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(db_query_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le)) * 1000) > bool 500) + (increase(pg_stat_database_deadlocks{datname="crypto_analytics"}[1h]) > bool 0) + (pg_locks_waiting_total > bool 0) + (((db_pool_active_connections / db_pool_max_connections) * 100) > bool 90))

panels.title: database queries duration count
panels.description: how long database queries take to execute

panels.title: Connection Pool Utilization
panels.description: Displays the percentage of the configured application-level connection pool currently in use, calculated as active pool connections divided by the maximum pool size, multiplied by 100. High utilization indicates the application is approaching the maximum number of concurrent database connections it is allowed to open, which can cause request queuing or connection timeout errors under load.

panels.title: Slowest Queries time
panels.description: Ranks the slowest SQL queries based on P95 execution time, grouped by query fingerprint or statement label. Calculated using histogram_quantile per query label, then topk(10, ...) to surface the worst offenders. This panel helps identify poorly optimized queries requiring indexing, query rewriting, or execution plan review.

panels.title: P50 Query Latency
panels.description: Median (50th percentile) database query execution time, computed with histogram_quantile over the db_query_duration histogram (buckets: 10/50/100/500/1000/2000ms). Half of all queries finish faster than this line - it represents typical/best-case latency, useful as a baseline to compare P90/P95/P99 against.

panels.title: P90 Query Latency
panels.description: 90th percentile database query execution time. 1 in 10 queries is slower than this line. A growing gap between P50 and P90 indicates a subset of queries (not the average) is degrading - usually a specific query pattern, missing index, or lock contention rather than general load.

panels.title: Read Distribution (Cache Efficiency)
panels.description: Shows what fraction of read requests PostgreSQL served from shared_buffers (in-memory cache hit) versus had to fetch from disk (cache miss), from pg_stat_database.blks_hit / blks_read. A healthy OLTP workload should sit above 99% cache hits; a falling ratio means the working set no longer fits in shared_buffers, directly explaining rising read latency and increased disk IO.

panels.title: Wait Event Distribution
panels.description: What active backends are currently blocked on, grouped by wait_event_type (Lock, IO, Client, BufferPin, Extension, LWLock, IPC, Timeout, Activity) from pg_stat_activity. This is the single fastest way to answer "why is the database slow right now": mostly Lock means contention/blocking sessions, mostly IO means disk-bound, mostly Client means the app/network is the bottleneck rather than Postgres itself.

panels.title: Write Distribution
panels.description: Breaks down write volume by operation type (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE from pg_stat_database.tup_*) alongside checkpoint and background-writer buffer flushes (pg_stat_bgwriter). A spike in one slice points to what is driving write load - e.g. a DELETE-heavy cleanup job versus a burst of forced checkpoints from max_wal_size being too small for the write rate.

panels.title: Disk IO
panels.description: Physical storage throughput and latency underneath PostgreSQL, from node_exporter, plus PostgreSQL-specific IO pressure signals: temp file writes (queries spilling sorts/hashes to disk - work_mem too small) and WAL throughput (write-heavy/replication load). If query latency rises while these climb, the database is disk-bound, not CPU or lock bound.

panels.title: Deadlock Analysis
panels.description: Rate of deadlocks detected by PostgreSQL (pg_stat_database.deadlocks), which fires when two or more transactions each hold a lock the other needs and neither can proceed - PostgreSQL kills one (the victim) to break the cycle. Any sustained non-zero rate here means the application has a lock-ordering bug that needs fixing, not just a database tuning issue.

panels.title: Connection Pool
panels.description: Prisma connection pool state over time: active (checked out and running a query), idle (open but unused), waiting (queries queued because every connection is busy), and the configured max. Populated by wirePrismaPoolMetrics() in src/metrics.ts, sourced from prisma.$metrics. Any sustained "waiting" above zero means requests are being queued behind the pool limit - the direct cause of request latency that isn't visible in query duration alone.

panels.title: Blocking Sessions
panels.description: Live table of every session currently blocked on a lock, paired with the session holding that lock, via pg_blocking_pids(). Populated by postgres_exporter (postgres-exporter-queries.yaml: pg_blocking_sessions). Answers "who is blocking whom, with what query, and for how long" - the first three questions during any lock-contention incident. Empty when nothing is blocked.

panels.title: Running Queries
panels.description: Every currently active (non-idle) backend from pg_stat_activity: PID, how long it has been running, state, application, database, and a normalized/truncated query fingerprint. Populated by postgres_exporter (pg_running_queries). This is the live "what is Postgres doing right now" view used to spot a runaway query before it becomes a long-running-query alert.

panels.title: Long Running Queries (> 2s)
panels.description: Subset of Running Queries that have executed longer than the configurable 30 second threshold (pg_running_queries_duration_seconds > 30). These are the queries most likely to be holding locks, consuming a connection-pool slot, or about to trigger an application-level timeout - the ones to investigate or kill first during an incident.

panels.title: Top 10 Slowest Queries (pg_stat_statements)
panels.description: The 10 normalized query shapes with the highest mean execution time, from pg_stat_statements (postgres_exporter: pg_stat_statements custom query). Unlike the app-level "database queries duration count" panel (which only sees queries the app explicitly timed), this sees every statement PostgreSQL itself executed, including ones issued by other tools/roles - the definitive answer to "which query should I optimize first."

panels.title: Redis Up
panels.description: Whether the Redis exporter can successfully reach the Redis instance. 1 means up, 0 means down.

panels.title: Redis Memory Used
panels.description: Displays the amount of memory currently used by Redis. Sustained growth toward the configured maxmemory limit may lead to evictions or OOM errors.

panels.title: Redis Connected Clients
panels.description: Displays the number of client connections currently open to Redis, including the app's cache client and BullMQ worker connections.

panels.title: Redis Ops/sec
panels.description: Displays the number of Redis commands processed per second. Useful for spotting traffic spikes from the price cache or BullMQ queue workers.

panels.title: Redis Cache Hit Ratio
panels.description: Displays the percentage of key lookups served from cache versus missed. Since priceService uses Redis as a cache, a dropping hit ratio means more requests are falling through to the external price API.

panels.title: Redis Evicted Keys Rate
panels.description: Displays the rate of keys evicted from Redis due to memory pressure. Any sustained non-zero value indicates Redis is hitting its maxmemory limit.
